standard.title: Causes and Effects of the Industrial Revolution
standard.description: the social, economic, political, technological and/or environmental causes and effects of the Industrial Revolution on Europe in the late 18th and 19th century
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can describe significant developments and their causes and effects in earlier periods (AC9HH8K03, AC9HH8K07). They have not yet examined the Industrial Revolution as a multi-causal, multi-domain transformation — the specific role of technology, the Agricultural Revolution preconditions, the spread of industrialisation across Europe, or how to evaluate the relative significance of multiple causes.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain how changes in technology led to the development of factories and industrialised cities, identify the spread of innovations across Europe and beyond, analyse the multiple factors that caused the Industrial Revolution, and evaluate the most significant effects across economic, social, political and environmental domains.

nodes.label: Preconditions for industrialisation — why Britain first
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify the preconditions that enabled industrialisation to begin in Britain and explain why industrialisation began there rather than elsewhere.
nodes.minimum_width: Students identify at least three preconditions for industrialisation in Britain (e.g. Agricultural Revolution, access to coal and iron, commercial infrastructure, Enlightenment ideas, imperial trade) and explain how each contributed.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe the Agricultural Revolution as releasing labour from the land; access to coal and iron ore as raw material foundations; the existing commercial infrastructure (banks, insurance, joint-stock companies); the legal framework for property rights and patents; Enlightenment ideas about progress and experimentation; the imperial trade network as both a source of capital and a market for manufactured goods; a growing population creating both labour supply and demand; explain why these conditions combined in Britain rather than France, the Netherlands or China.
wider: Evaluate the relative weight of different preconditions — which was most important? Develop a supported argument and anticipate objections

Examine why China, which had many of the technological preconditions, did not industrialise first — exploring what this comparison reveals about the relative importance of social, political and economic conditions vs purely technological ones
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding why industrialisation began in Britain rather than elsewhere is the prerequisite for understanding both the technology node (N2) and the significance evaluation in N4. Students who treat the Industrial Revolution as simply 'machines were invented' cannot explain why it was transformative or how it spread, nor can they engage the multi-causal analysis the descriptor demands.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly treat the Industrial Revolution as a story of invention (steam engine → factories) without understanding the social, economic and political preconditions that made invention commercially viable and transformative. Making the preconditions explicit is the scaffold for multi-causal analysis throughout the standard.

success_criteria: Identifies at least three preconditions for industrialisation and explains how each contributed
Explains why industrialisation began in Britain rather than other European nations

nodes.label: Technology and the factory system — steam, iron and textiles
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how key technological changes — steam-driven machinery, iron and steel production, railways — led to the development of factories and industrialised cities.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe the steam engine as the core technology, explain how it enabled factories and railways, and describe the resulting growth of industrial cities.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe the development of steam power (Watt's improvements, stationary engines in factories, mobile engines in railways and ships); the role of iron and steel production in enabling machinery, railways and buildings; the textile industry (spinning jenny, power loom) as the first industrialised factory sector; how railways connected industrial cities and created integrated national markets; how steam power in ships enabled global trade expansion; explain the city-factory connection — factories concentrated workers in urban areas, cities grew to house and supply them.
wider: Examine a specific technological innovation in depth — e.g. the Rocket locomotive (Stephenson, 1829) — and trace its effects across multiple domains (transport, manufacturing, settlement patterns, trade)
Investigate the spread of steam technology beyond Britain to Europe, the USA and Japan — examining how technology transfer happened and what adapted or changed in different national contexts

response_modes.reason: Students commonly describe the steam engine as important without understanding the mechanism — how it enabled the factory system (replacing human and water power), how railways created integrated markets, how the combination of factory and city growth is causally connected. Making these connections explicit builds the causal picture the descriptor requires.

success_criteria: Describes steam power and at least one other key technology, explaining how each enabled industrial development
Explains the connection between factory growth and the development of industrial cities

nodes.label: The spread of industrialisation — Europe, USA and Japan
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe how industrialisation spread from Britain to Europe, the USA and Japan, and identify the spread of key innovations (steam power, iron and steel, transport, new chemicals).
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe industrialisation spreading to at least two other regions (e.g. Europe, USA, Japan) and identify at least two innovations that spread with it.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe the spread to continental Europe (Belgium, France, Germany) from the 1820s–50s; the American industrialisation (New England textile mills, railroad expansion, Civil War steel production); the Japanese Meiji Restoration (1868) as a deliberately state-directed industrialisation; the role of technology transfer — deliberate copying, patent breaking, hiring of British engineers; the spread of railways, steel production, chemical industries; explain what was similar and different about industrialisation in different national contexts.
wider: Compare the Japanese Meiji industrialisation with the British model — examining how state-directed industrialisation produced a different social and political outcome to Britain's more market-driven process
Examine how the spread of industrialisation connected to European imperial expansion — the industrial powers had major military and economic advantages that shaped the rest of the 19th century

response_modes.reason: Students commonly treat industrialisation as a British story without understanding it as a global process of uneven development. Multiple national examples build the comparative picture required by the descriptor.

success_criteria: Describes the spread of industrialisation to at least two regions beyond Britain
Identifies at least two innovations that spread with industrialisation and describes how each spread

nodes.label: Effects of the Industrial Revolution — evaluating significance across domains
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the range of effects of the Industrial Revolution — economic, social, political, environmental — and evaluate which effects were most significant.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe at least three distinct effects across different domains (e.g. economic growth, changing working conditions, growth of the middle class, environmental impacts) and make a judgement about which was most significant.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe effects across all major domains — economic growth and GDP rise; changing social structures (growth of industrial working class and middle class, decline of artisan craft economy); changing working conditions (factory discipline, long hours, child labour, urbanisation); new political ideas (socialism, trade unionism, chartism) emerging in response to industrial conditions; environmental impacts (pollution, deforestation, urban squalor); the rise of imperialism as industrial nations competed for markets and raw materials; evaluate significance — which effect had the greatest long-term consequences — and defend a position with evidence.
wider: Examine the environmental effects of industrialisation in depth — urban pollution, river contamination, coal mining landscapes — and connect to contemporary environmental concerns

Evaluate the 'standard of living debate' — did industrialisation improve or worsen living standards for the majority of British people in the 19th century? Examine the evidence and the historiographical debate
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The significance evaluation task — which effects mattered most — is a genuine analytical challenge where different frameworks (short-term vs long-term, economic vs social, Britain vs global) produce legitimately different answers. The standard of living debate is a well-developed historiographical dispute that models how historians use evidence differently.

response_modes.reason: Evaluating significance requires students to draw on knowledge from all domains — economic, social, political, environmental — and synthesise into a supported judgement. This is the full-descriptor integration task.

success_criteria: Describes effects of the Industrial Revolution across at least three domains
Evaluates which effect was most significant and defends the judgement with evidence
